lanes.label: building it with an AI assistant

ideas.title: Your garden, month by month
ideas.tagline: A planting calendar that knows your weather.
ideas.describe: Tell it where you live and what you want to grow. It turns that into a calendar of real jobs — sow this now, water twice a week, pick before the heat — instead of a generic guide written for another country.
steps: Write down the ten things your household actually eats.
Get the local weather for the next three months and mark the hot and cold weeks.
Match each crop to a planting window and a watering rhythm.
Print it, stick it on the fridge, and adjust it after the first month.

pattern: Ask questions over your own notes

ideas.helps: Households growing food on a balcony, a roof or a small plot, where the advice online assumes a different climate.
ideas.watch: Weather data gives averages, not your yard. The first season will be wrong in places, so treat the calendar as a draft you keep correcting.

ideas.title: Cook what you already have
ideas.tagline: Type what's in the fridge, get tonight's dinner.
ideas.describe: Most food gets thrown out because nobody can think of a meal at seven in the evening. List what's in the fridge and cupboard, and get three things you can cook tonight with steps short enough to follow while tired.
needs: A list of what's in the kitchen
steps: Keep a running list of what's in the fridge — one line each.
Add the things that always fail: allergies, no oven, twenty minutes max.
Ask for three meals using only what's on the list.
Save the ones the family actually ate; they become the default rotation.

pattern: Answer from a small private list, not the whole internet

ideas.helps: Anyone cooking for a family on a tight week, where the food is already bought and the hard part is deciding.
ideas.watch: It will suggest combinations that sound wrong. Keep the three meals the household actually ate and quietly drop the rest.

ideas.title: What things cost this week
ideas.tagline: Twenty prices, tracked until the pattern shows.
ideas.describe: Pick the twenty things you buy every week — eggs, oil, chicken, tomatoes. Note the price each time you shop. After a month you can see what is creeping up, which shop is cheaper, and where the money actually goes.
steps: List twenty staples and the shop you buy each one from.
Write the price and the date, every shop, for four weeks.
Chart each item as a single line — the jump will be obvious.
Share the shortlist of 'buy this here, that there' with family.

pattern: Turn a plain table into charts

ideas.helps: People who shop weekly and suspect the bill is rising faster than the wages, but have no record to prove it.
ideas.watch: Twenty items is the limit. Track more and you stop tracking. Note which shop each price came from, or the line means nothing.

ideas.title: A patient baking coach
ideas.tagline: For the recipe you keep failing at.
ideas.describe: Sourdough, pastries, bread — the kind of thing where the recipe assumes you already know what 'until it looks right' means. A coach that answers the one question you have right now, with photos, and never makes you feel stupid.
steps: Pick one recipe and make it badly once, on purpose.
Write down exactly where it went wrong — the dough, the oven, the timing.
Build a page of the five questions you always have, with photos of each stage.
Test it on someone else who has never baked; fix the part they got stuck on.

prompt: Act as a Beginner Sourdough Starter Coach

ideas.helps: Someone learning a craft alone, where the recipe assumes a teacher standing next to them.
ideas.watch: A coach can describe 'until it looks right' but cannot feel the dough. Expect to fail the first three loaves; that is the lesson.

ideas.title: Never overspend on a celebration again
ideas.tagline: Weddings, Eid, Christmas, birthdays — one budget.
ideas.describe: Plan a celebration properly: who you're buying for, a limit per person, what's already bought, and what's left. It adds up as you go and warns you while there's still time to change your mind, not afterwards.
steps: Write the list of people and a limit for each.
Add what you've already bought and what it cost.
Watch the running total against the limit, not the wish list.
Keep it for next year — most of the list is the same.

prompt: Holiday Gift Plan and Budget Builder

ideas.helps: Anyone planning a wedding, Eid, Christmas or a birthday round, where the spending happens in small amounts and the total arrives at the end.
ideas.watch: The limit per person is the whole point. Set it after the shopping and this is only a folder of receipts.

ideas.title: Who owes what at home
ideas.tagline: One list, no group-chat argument.
ideas.describe: Rent, electricity, internet, water, the man who fixes the boiler. Everyone in the flat or the family sees what's paid, what's late, and who owes what — settled with a screenshot instead of a three-day conversation.
steps: List every recurring bill, its amount, and its due date.
Split each one by whatever rule your household actually uses.
Show one total per person and one 'paid' tick per bill.
Send a reminder three days before, not the day after.

pattern: Sums and reminders over a small table

ideas.helps: Shared flats and extended families where one person pays and three people forget.
ideas.watch: It records what was paid, not who is right. Agree what counts as a shared bill before the first entry, or the argument moves into the app.

ideas.title: Prices in the money you think in
ideas.tagline: Earn in one currency, spend in another.
ideas.describe: A shopping list that shows every price in both currencies at today's rate, with both totals. For people sending money home, working abroad, or budgeting for a trip — so the number on the shelf stops being a riddle.
steps: Pick the two currencies and the day's rate.
Enter prices as you shop; show both amounts side by side.
Show the running total in both, and the difference from last week.
Keep the last rate on the phone so it still works when the signal drops.
ideas.helps: People earning in one currency and spending in another, sending money home, working abroad, or saving for a trip.
ideas.watch: Rates move daily and the card fee hides behind the headline rate. Show the date of the rate and the fee, or the number lies.

ideas.title: A renovation that stays on budget
ideas.tagline: Kitchen, bathroom, or one wall of paint.
ideas.describe: Plan the job in the order it actually happens: what gets ripped out, what gets bought, who does which part, how long each waits for the other. A running total and photos at each stage, so problems show up early instead of on the last day.
needs: Photos of the room as it is
steps: Photograph the room and write down what's wrong with it.
List the stages in order and what has to be bought before each one.
Add who does each stage and how many days it takes.
Photograph after every stage; the photos are your proof when something fails.

prompt: Kitchen Remodel Timeline and Budget Plan

ideas.helps: Anyone running a kitchen, bathroom or single-room job with several trades who each wait for the one before.
ideas.watch: The plan is the easy part. Build in a two-week slip and a ten per cent contingency, or the first delay takes the budget with it.

ideas.title: Receipts and warranties that don't vanish
ideas.tagline: Photograph it once, forget it safely.
ideas.describe: Photograph a receipt and it remembers what you bought, where, how long the warranty lasts, and reminds you a week before it ends. No more drawers of faded paper, and no more paying for a repair that was still covered.
steps: Photograph every receipt for a month.
Record item, shop, date, price and warranty length.
Sort by the date the warranty ends, not the date you bought it.
Set one reminder a week before each expiry.
ideas.helps: Households with a drawer of faded receipts and no idea which appliances are still covered.
ideas.watch: A photograph of a receipt fades too if it is out of focus. Check the date and the shop are readable before you file it.

ideas.title: Where your water and power go
ideas.tagline: One number a week, and the bill stops being a surprise.
ideas.describe: Type the number off the meter once a week. It draws the line, shows your worst week, and tells you when a bill doesn't match what you actually used — before you pay it.
steps: Find the meter and photograph where the number sits.
Enter the reading on the same day each week.
Compare the change to last month and to last year.
When a bill arrives, check it against the readings before paying.

pattern: Charts from a handful of numbers

ideas.helps: Tenants and owners whose bill arrives as one number with no explanation of where it came from.
ideas.watch: A weekly reading catches a leak, not a habit. It cannot tell you which appliance is expensive without a second meter.

ideas.title: Car care without the guesswork
ideas.tagline: Service history, renewals, and the tyre that's been low for months.
ideas.describe: Everything about the car in one place: oil changes, tyres, registration renewal, the mechanic's number. Reminders arrive early enough to book something, instead of the morning the paper expires.
steps: Write down make, model, year and plate.
Add past services with dates and mileage.
Add renewals and the date each one expires.
Set reminders thirty days before, not on the day.
ideas.helps: People who keep a car running on memory: the service, the registration, the tyre that has been low for months.
ideas.watch: A reminder is only as good as the date you entered. Photograph the paperwork when you file it, not a year later.

ideas.title: Plan the family trip once
ideas.tagline: One plan everyone can actually see.
ideas.describe: Dates, budget, who's driving, where you stop, what to pack. Everyone gets the same plan on their phone, the packing list ticks itself off, and nobody asks 'what time are we leaving?' for the ninth time.
steps: Agree the dates and the total you're willing to spend.
List the stops in order with driving times between them.
Build one packing list per person, shared, tickable.
Send the same link to everyone and keep it as the single truth.

prompt: Family Road Trip Plan and Packing List

ideas.helps: Families where one person plans everything and everyone else asks the same four questions.
ideas.watch: One plan only works if everyone can open it. Decide who owns the dates and the budget before you share the link.

ideas.title: What do we do with the kids this weekend?
ideas.tagline: Cheap and nearby, filtered by age and patience.
ideas.describe: A short list of free or cheap things happening around you, filtered by the children's ages and how far you're willing to drive. Updated on Thursday evening, when the question is actually asked.
steps: Collect the places: parks, libraries, playgrounds, free museum days.
Tag each with age range, cost, and drive time.
Pick five for the weekend and say why each one fits.
Add what you actually went to; drop the ones that disappointed.

pattern: Suggests options from a fixed list, not from thin air

ideas.helps: Parents on a Thursday evening with two days to fill and no intention of spending much.
ideas.watch: Local listings go stale. Confirm the place is open the week you publish it, or the list becomes a list of disappointments.

ideas.title: No more missed school forms
ideas.tagline: Every trip, exam, fee and permission slip, in one place.
ideas.describe: Each child's school dates in one list you export to the phone's calendar once — so the reminders become the phone's job and the paperwork stays yours. Photograph the letter that came home in the bag and it goes where it belongs.
steps: Collect every paper that came home this term.
Add each date, what it needs, and how much it costs.
Export the whole list to the phone calendar in one go — that's where the reminders live.
Share the calendar with whoever does the school run.
ideas.helps: Parents juggling two or three schools, where the letter arrives in a bag and the date is next week.
ideas.watch: Schools change dates without telling the calendar. Re-check the term dates at the start of each term, not once a year.

ideas.title: Chores and pocket money, settled
ideas.tagline: The board does the arguing.
ideas.describe: A simple board where each child ticks off their jobs, watches the total grow, and sees how close they are to whatever they're saving for. Removes the weekly negotiation from your evening.
steps: List the jobs and what each is worth.
Give each child a goal with a price, so saving has a point.
Tick the jobs off together at the end of the day.
Pay out on a fixed day, every time, no exceptions.
ideas.helps: Households where the same argument about jobs and pocket money happens every Sunday.
ideas.watch: It settles the total, not the fairness. Agree the rate per job with the children once, in writing, or the board becomes the argument.

ideas.title: Medicine reminders that survive a bad day
ideas.tagline: For a parent who isn't on the phone all day.
ideas.describe: A tablet left on the kitchen counter showing today's doses in huge type, with one button to confirm each. The phone's own alarm does the reminding — this makes the record readable to whoever is checking in.
needs: A phone alarm for each dose
steps: List each medicine, dose and time — with the actual pill in front of you.
Set one alarm per dose on the phone itself. That's what actually reminds.
Make the tablet screen show today's doses with one enormous button each.
Test it with the person who'll use it, and follow their words, not yours.
ideas.helps: Older parents living alone, or anyone whose doses are remembered by a relative rather than by them.
ideas.watch: This is a record, not a medical device. Keep the phone alarm as the reminder; the screen is for whoever checks in.

ideas.title: Ten thousand steps, without the guilt
ideas.tagline: One route, honestly tracked.
ideas.describe: Pick a route near home, count how often you actually walk it, and see the month at a glance. No streaks to break, no subscription, no shame — just the truth, which turns out to be motivating enough.
steps: Walk three routes and time them.
Pick the one you'd do on a bad day, not the best day.
Mark each walk with one tap — that's the whole interface.
Look at the month on the first of the next one.
ideas.helps: People who want to move more and have already abandoned two apps that scolded them.
ideas.watch: Honest counting means some weeks look bad. Hide those and the month stops telling you anything.

ideas.title: Every appointment in one place
ideas.tagline: So you can answer 'when did this start?'
ideas.describe: Doctor, dentist, lab results, prescriptions. Who you saw, what they said, what happens next. Five minutes after each visit saves an hour of reconstruction at the next one — and stops you repeating the same tests.
steps: Add the last six months of visits from memory and paperwork.
For each: date, who, what was said, what's next.
Photograph prescriptions and lab sheets into the same entry.
Before the next visit, read the previous entry out loud.
ideas.helps: Anyone with a long-running condition, or caring for someone who sees four different doctors.
ideas.watch: It holds health details. Keep it on your own device, and never paste a whole record into a public page or a group chat.

ideas.title: A study plan that survives real life
ideas.tagline: Short sittings, and a plan that moves when you miss a day.
ideas.describe: Enter the exam date and the chapters. It splits the work into sittings short enough to actually start, then reshuffles the remaining days when life gets in the way instead of collapsing.
steps: List the chapters and estimate how long each really takes.
Divide into twenty-five minute sittings with a real break.
Mark each sitting done, and let missed ones move, never vanish.
Do one full past paper a week before the date.

prompt: Reading Plan and Page Pace Planner

ideas.helps: Students revising alone, and adults sitting a qualification around a job.
ideas.watch: The reshuffle is the useful part. A plan that never moves is a plan you have already abandoned.

ideas.title: Someone to practise English with
ideas.tagline: Five minutes a day, out loud, without embarrassment.
ideas.describe: Speak for five minutes about ordinary things — ordering food, a job interview, a phone call to the bank — and get a gentle correction on the two things that matter most. Practising with a machine is easier than practising with a person who might laugh.
steps: Pick five situations you actually avoid because of the language.
Write one short scene for each.
Speak the scene out loud and get two corrections, no more.
Repeat the same scene in a week; notice it got easier.

publish: Free tier for a small server

ideas.helps: Recent arrivals, and anyone who reads English better than they speak it in front of a person.
ideas.watch: A machine will not teach the rhythm of a real conversation. Use it to lose the fear, then practise with a person.

ideas.title: A beginner's coach for the thing you keep postponing
ideas.tagline: Chess, ukulele, sewing, swimming — twenty minutes at a time.
ideas.describe: Instead of a hundred videos and no order, one small next step, checked. It notices what you got wrong last time and builds the next session around it, the way a patient teacher would.
steps: Write the one thing you want to be able to do in a month.
Break it into twenty-minute sessions that each end with something finished.
Record each session and ask what went wrong, specifically.
Re-test the first thing you learned every two weeks.

prompt: Act as a Beginner Chess Opening Coach
prompt2: Act as a Beginner Ukulele Coach

ideas.helps: Adults who have bought the instrument, the board or the sewing machine, and stopped at the third session.
ideas.watch: One small step is the whole design. If it starts offering a curriculum, it has become the hundred videos again.

ideas.title: Teach one thing, learn another
ideas.tagline: A swap board for your neighbourhood.
ideas.describe: A board where someone posts 'I can fix bikes, I want to learn to cook' and gets matched with the person next door who wants the opposite. No money changes hands, and the neighbourhood gets a little less anonymous.
steps: Ask twenty neighbours for one thing they can teach and one they want.
Write each as a pair, in their own words.
Match opposites, and introduce them with one message.
Keep a public list of what worked, so the next match is easier.
ideas.helps: Neighbours with a skill and no outlet, and neighbours with a need and no money for lessons.
ideas.watch: Matching strangers needs a public place and a first meeting. Do not publish phone numbers; let the board hold the introduction.

ideas.title: Lost and found for your street
ideas.tagline: Keys, a school bag, a cat.
ideas.describe: A page of things found on the street — keys, a school bag, a cat — that you link once in the building group. People claim by describing something that isn't in the photo, and the post comes down when it's returned.
needs: A place to leave found items
steps: Agree one safe place where found things are kept.
Post a photo, the place, and the date — never the full address.
Let people claim by describing something not visible in the photo.
Delete the post when it's returned.

data: Free form backend for static sites, 250/month

ideas.helps: Streets and buildings where things are found every week and the group chat scrolls past them in a day.
ideas.watch: Do not publish a photo that proves ownership. Ask the claimer to describe something that is not in the picture.

ideas.title: The building noticeboard, but readable
ideas.tagline: Water cuts, repairs, rules, meetings.
ideas.describe: One place for the things a building actually needs to tell everyone: when the water is off, which lift is broken, what changed about parking. Sorted by date, written in plain language, and the caretaker can post in seconds.
steps: Ask the caretaker what he repeats most often by voice.
Turn the five most common messages into fixed templates.
Post each with a date and an expiry — old notices disappear by themselves.
Print a QR code for the entrance.
ideas.helps: Buildings with a caretaker, a group chat, and no single place where the water-cut notice survives.
ideas.watch: It only works if the caretaker can post in under a minute. Test that first; a board nobody updates is worse than the chat.

ideas.title: Is the water out on your street too?
ideas.tagline: One tap, one message to the group, no phone numbers exposed.
ideas.describe: Two buttons: water, power. Tap one and it opens WhatsApp with the message already written — the street, the time, how long it's been off. The record builds itself in the group chat, and the next person can see instantly whether it's just them.
needs: A building or street group chat
steps: Pick two buttons: water, power — nothing else.
Write one message template with the street and the time filled in.
Make each button open WhatsApp with that message ready to send.
Pin the page in the group so it's one tap away the next time something goes.
ideas.helps: Streets where the water or power goes off and everyone asks the group chat whether it is just them.
ideas.watch: Two buttons and nothing else. Every extra field is a reason not to report, and an unreported outage is invisible.

ideas.title: Report it once, properly
ideas.tagline: A pothole, a broken light, dumped rubbish.
ideas.describe: Photograph the problem and it records the location and date and writes the message to whoever is responsible, in the form they expect. Keeps a record, so 'we already reported it' becomes a fact instead of a memory.
steps: Find the office that actually handles this, and how they take reports.
Write the message template once, with placeholders.
Attach photo, date and location automatically.
Log every report so you can follow up in two weeks.

pattern: Fetch and fill forms from a page

ideas.helps: Residents who report the same pothole or broken light three times and get nowhere.
ideas.watch: The office may ignore email. Find the channel they actually read, a form, a number or a council app, before building the message.

ideas.title: Fill the volunteer rota without twenty phone calls
ideas.tagline: For the centre, the mosque, the school.
ideas.describe: The organisation posts the shifts it needs, and people claim one through a short form. You get an email per claim and update the page once. Replaces the group chat where the same four people always end up doing everything.
steps: List the shifts for one month, with times and how many people each needs.
Put a short claim form on the page — name, shift, phone.
Update the page once a day and show what's still empty; visible gaps get filled.
Thank people by name afterwards; that's what brings them back.

data: Free form backend, emails you each claim

ideas.helps: Small organisations, a centre, a mosque or a school, where the same four people fill every rota.
ideas.watch: Publishing shifts is easy; reminding people is the work. Decide who sends the reminder before you launch it.

ideas.title: Invoices for people who fix things
ideas.tagline: A plumber, electrician or painter, on their phone.
ideas.describe: Make a proper quote or invoice in two minutes, send it on WhatsApp, and keep a record of who paid. Turns a paper notebook and a vague memory into something you can show the tax office or a customer who 'never received' it.
steps: List your ten usual jobs and what you charge.
Make one screen: customer, job, parts, total.
Send as a clean PDF or a link; keep the copy.
Mark paid or unpaid, and who owes you from last month.
ideas.helps: Plumbers, electricians and painters who quote on WhatsApp and remember payments in a notebook.
ideas.watch: A clean invoice does not make a customer pay. Keep the record anyway; it is the thing that ends the argument.

ideas.title: A price list that updates itself
ideas.tagline: For home bakers and cooks.
ideas.describe: Photograph today's cakes, set the prices, and share one link. Orders arrive as a list instead of scattered across five chats and a phone that never stops ringing — and yesterday's sold-out cake disappears from the page.
steps: Photograph five things you make, on a clean background.
Set one price each and how much notice you need.
Publish one page with a WhatsApp order button.
Turn items off when sold out — that's the whole trick.
ideas.helps: Home bakers and cooks selling through five chats and a phone that rings during dinner.
ideas.watch: Yesterday's cake has to disappear. If the page is not updated the next morning, it is selling something you cannot make.

ideas.title: A first CV when you have no experience
ideas.tagline: School, volunteering, odd jobs — it counts.
ideas.describe: Answer simple questions about school, volunteering and the jobs nobody called jobs. It turns them into a clean one-page CV and a short message you can send to an employer, in the format people here actually read.
needs: A list of what you've done
steps: List every school, course, volunteer day and paid job, however small.
For each, write one line about what you were responsible for.
Choose a simple single-page layout that prints well in black and white.
Write a four-line message to send with it — that's the part that gets replies.
ideas.helps: School leavers and people returning to work who have done plenty and can name none of it as experience.
ideas.watch: Do not let it invent experience. Every line has to survive a question in an interview.

ideas.title: A checklist for confusing paperwork
ideas.tagline: Visas, insurance, permits, registration.
ideas.describe: Paste the requirements once and get a checklist with the documents, the dates and what's still missing. The point isn't the list — it's not discovering the missing paper at the counter, on the last day.
steps: Copy the official requirements exactly, including the wording.
Turn each into a tick with the document it needs.
Add the office hours, the fee and the deadline.
Photograph each document as you gather it, into the same entry.
ideas.helps: Anyone facing a visa, an insurance claim, a permit or a registration where one missing paper resets the whole visit.
ideas.watch: Official requirements change without notice. Date the checklist and re-read the source the week of the appointment.

formats: a printable sheet for the fridge
a QR code taped to the door
constraints: under two hours a week to run
using no paid tools at all
on a phone that cost less than the dinner
by two people who have never met
